cases.oracle_error: could not build proof via 1.1.1.1:53: The server provided a response we could not understand
cases.reason: NODATA at a DNAME owner name, proved by an NSEC3 whose type bitmap is DNAME RRSIG only. The name is a DNAME, so querying TXT at the owner itself returns nothing, while querying TXT below it redirects. Compare with the successful wildcard_a.wildcard_b.dname_test case, which is the same DNAME exercised from below.

cases.oracle_error: could not build proof via 1.1.1.1:53: The server indicated the records we needed were not DNSSEC-authenticated
cases.reason: Unsigned zone. google.com publishes no DS at .com, so there is no chain to validate and the proof builder correctly refuses rather than falling back to insecure. A port must fail here, and must fail for this reason, not because a signature did not verify.

cases.oracle_error: could not build proof via 1.1.1.1:53: The server provided a response we could not understand
cases.reason: NODATA, not NXDOMAIN. The name exists in a signed RSASHA256 zone and has A and AAAA, but no TXT. Proved by an NSEC record whose type bitmap lists A AAAA RRSIG NSEC and omits TXT. The oracle cannot distinguish this from other parse failures and says 'a response we could not understand'. A port SHOULD tell NODATA apart from a broken response; this case is here precisely to make that difference testable.

Valid. Encodes bc1qztwy6xen3zdtt7z0vrgapmjtfz8acjkfp5fp7l. The BIP notes the second TXT record, which does not start case-insensitively with 'bitcoin:', is ignored. Signatures were valid on 2025-08-07.

Valid. Encodes BC1QYYQ734DCNHHCWYW8YJXSWXG4P7K9NXU0QT84QZ. This is the explicit override of a wildcard, so the name itself exists and no wildcard non-existence proof is needed. Signatures were valid on 2025-08-06.

Valid. Encodes both bc1qztwy6xen3zdtt7z0vrgapmjtfz8acjkfp5fp7l and a BOLT 12 offer. This is the wildcard-published case: the name is served by a cross-domain wildcard CNAME, so the proof must carry the NSEC3 showing there is no more specific override. Compare byte for byte against case 05, which is this proof with that NSEC3 removed.

INVALID per the BIP. It is a cryptographically VALID DNSSEC proof, so a pure dnssec-prover-style chain validator is expected to ACCEPT it. It must be rejected by BIP 353 layer validation, because it contains two TXT records that both start case-insensitively with 'bitcoin:' and BIP 353 permits exactly one. The live records differ only in case ('BiTcOiN:?BC=' versus 'bitcoin:?bc='), which is the whole point: the check is case-insensitive.

INVALID per the BIP. Same name and same payload as case 03, but the NSEC3 record required to prove there is no override to the wildcard CNAME entry has been removed. A chain validator must refuse this: without that NSEC3 the resolver could be hiding a more specific record. This is the single most valuable case in the corpus, because the naive way to write a validator is to check every signature present and forget to check that a required denial-of-existence record is present at all.
